passages.title: Rereading versus retrieval practice
text: Researchers tested whether the way students study a text affects how much of it they remember later. In a hypothetical experiment, 128 undergraduates read a 600-word passage about tidal ecosystems for 6 minutes. They were then randomly assigned to one of two study conditions. In the rereading condition, participants read the passage twice more, 6 minutes each time. In the retrieval-practice condition, participants spent the same two 6-minute periods writing down from memory as much of the passage as they could, with no feedback. Immediately afterward every participant predicted, on a 0–100 scale, what percentage of the passage they would remember in one week.

Within each study condition, half of the participants (32 per group) took a final free-recall test 5 minutes later and half took it one week later. Two raters, blind to condition, scored each recall protocol for the percentage of the passage's 25 idea units it contained (inter-rater agreement r = 0.91). Figure 1 shows the mean percentage recalled in each of the four groups; standard deviations were about 11 points in every group.

A 2 × 2 analysis of variance found a main effect of retention interval, F(1, 124) = 139.9, p < .001, and an interaction between study condition and retention interval, F(1, 124) = 16.9, p < .001. The main effect of study condition was not significant (F < 1). Participants in the rereading condition predicted that they would recall 70% of the passage after one week; those in the retrieval-practice condition predicted 50%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Mean percentage of idea units recalled, by study condition and retention interval (standard deviations about 11 points in every group).
figures.alt: Bar chart with two pairs of bars. After 5 minutes: rereading 71 percent, retrieval practice 63 percent. After one week: rereading 40 percent, retrieval practice 48 percent.

passages.source: Hypothetical experiment written for this app. Its design resembles published retrieval-practice studies (e.g., Roediger HL, Karpicke JD. Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science. 2006;17:249–255); the numbers are invented.

items.stem: The independent variables in the experiment are:

options.B: study condition and percentage of idea units recalled

why_correct: An independent variable is one the researchers set. They assigned participants to a study condition (rereading or retrieval practice) and to a retention interval (5 minutes or one week), giving a 2 × 2 design with four groups.
Percentage recalled is the dependent variable, measured to see the effect of those manipulations; predicted recall is an additional measured variable.
The passage's own analysis confirms the structure: the ANOVA tests the effects of study condition, retention interval, and their interaction.

why_wrong.B: Percentage recalled was measured, not manipulated; it is the dependent variable.
why_wrong.C: Predicted recall was a rating participants gave, not something the researchers assigned.
why_wrong.D: Both of these are outcomes recorded from participants; neither was manipulated.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: a dependent variable listed as independent
error_types.C: reversed relationship: a measured rating treated as a manipulation
error_types.D: reversed relationship: two measured outcomes treated as manipulations

items.takeaway: Independent variables are the ones the experimenter manipulates; what is measured afterward is the dependent variable.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): independent variable (manipulated by the experimenter) versus dependent variable (measured); random assignment.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern of results in Figure 1?

options.A: Retrieval practice produced better recall at both intervals
options.B: Rereading produced better recall at both intervals
options.C: Rereading was better after 5 minutes, but retrieval practice was better after one week
options.D: The two study methods did not differ at either interval

why_correct: Read the bars: at 5 minutes rereading (71%) is above retrieval practice (63%); at one week the order reverses, retrieval practice (48%) above rereading (40%).
This crossover is what the significant interaction in the passage reports: the effect of study method depends on when memory is tested.

The non-significant main effect of study condition fits too: averaged over both intervals the methods come out equal (55.5% each), because the 8-point advantage runs in opposite directions at the two intervals.

why_wrong.A: At 5 minutes the rereading group recalled more (71% versus 63%), so retrieval practice was not better at both intervals.
why_wrong.B: At one week the rereading group recalled less (40% versus 48%).
why_wrong.D: The groups differed by 8 points at each interval, in opposite directions, and the interaction was significant.

error_types.B: misread graph: the one-week bars reversed

items.takeaway: A crossover between conditions across levels of a second variable is an interaction: the effect of one variable depends on the other.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): reading experimental results; interpreting group differences.
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 13.1 One-Way ANOVA (2023): analysis of variance compares group means using an F statistic.

items.stem: The gap between what the rereading group predicted (70%) and what it actually recalled after one week (40%) best illustrates:

options.B: a metacognitive illusion in which the fluency of rereading is mistaken for durable learning
options.D: proactive interference from the first reading

why_correct: Rereading makes a text feel familiar and easy to process. People read that fluency as a sign that the material is well learned, and so they overestimate how much will survive a delay.
The retrieval-practice group, who had just struggled to recall the passage, had direct evidence of what they did not know; their prediction (50%) was close to their actual one-week recall (48%).
Judgements of learning that track familiarity rather than retrievability are a well-documented source of poor study choices.

why_wrong.A: The spacing effect is better retention when study sessions are spread out over time; the sessions here were back to back in both conditions, and the gap concerns prediction versus performance.
why_wrong.C: State-dependent memory is better recall when a person's internal state at retrieval matches the state at encoding; nothing in the design manipulated internal state.
why_wrong.D: Proactive interference is older material hindering recall of newer material; rereading the same passage does not create competing content, and interference would not explain an over-confident prediction.

error_types.A: out of scope: a scheduling effect, not a judgement error
error_types.C: out of scope: no state manipulation in the design
error_types.D: wrong formula: interference requires competing material

items.takeaway: Ease of processing during restudy inflates judgements of learning; retrieval practice gives more accurate self-assessment and better long-term retention.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.4 Ways to Enhance Memory (2020): rehearsal, practice quizzes and spaced study as memory strategies.

Koriat A, Bjork RA. Illusions of competence in monitoring one's knowledge during study. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. 2005;31(2):187–194: judgements of learning made while the material is in view instil an unwarranted sense of competence.

Roediger HL, Karpicke JD. Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science. 2006;17(3):249–255: repeated study produced higher predicted recall but lower delayed recall than repeated testing.

items.stem: The reported interaction, F(1, 124) = 16.9, p < .001, means that:

options.A: the effect of study method depended on the retention interval, and a difference in pattern this large would be very unlikely if there were no true interaction
options.B: the probability that the null hypothesis is true is less than 0.001
options.C: retrieval practice improved recall by 16.2 percentage points
options.D: the result would be obtained in 99.9% of replications

why_correct: An interaction term tests whether the effect of one independent variable differs across levels of the other. Here the study-method difference reversed between 5 minutes and one week.
The p-value is the probability of observing an interaction at least this strong if, in the population, there were none. Below .001, the observed crossover is very unlikely to be a chance pattern.
The F statistic is a ratio of the variance explained by the interaction to the error variance; it is not a percentage or an effect size.

why_wrong.B: A p-value is the probability of the data (or more extreme data) given the null hypothesis, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true; the latter would require a Bayesian analysis with prior probabilities.
why_wrong.C: F = 16.9 is a variance ratio, not a difference in recall; the one-week advantage of retrieval practice in Figure 1 is 8 points, and averaged across intervals the two methods tie.
why_wrong.D: A p-value says nothing about the probability of replication; replication depends on effect size, sample size and the study's design.

error_types.B: reversed relationship: the conditional probability inverted
error_types.C: misread graph: a test statistic read as an effect size
error_types.D: wrong formula: p-value confused with replication probability

items.takeaway: p is the chance of data this extreme if the null were true; it is not the chance the null is true, an effect size, or a replication rate.
sources: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 9.4 Rare Events, the Sample, and the Decision and Conclusion (2023): the p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed.
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, 13.2 The F Distribution and the F-Ratio (2023): F is the ratio of between-group to within-group variance.
OpenStax Psychology 2e, 2.3 Analyzing Findings (2020): statistical significance.

items.stem: The decline in recall between 5 minutes and one week seen in both study conditions is best described as:

options.A: retroactive interference caused by the final test
options.B: encoding failure, because the passage never entered long-term memory
options.C: anterograde amnesia for material learned in the laboratory
options.D: normal forgetting of the kind described by the forgetting curve

why_correct: Memory for newly learned material drops quickly in the hours and days after learning and then declines more slowly, the pattern Ebbinghaus first charted as the forgetting curve. A week is long enough for much of that early loss.
Both groups show it; retrieval practice slowed the loss (63% to 48%) more than rereading did (71% to 40%), but did not prevent it.
The decline is ordinary storage decay plus interference from everything learned in the intervening week, not a defect of the participants or the design.

why_wrong.A: Retroactive interference is newer learning hindering recall of older material; the final test is the measurement itself, taken once, and cannot interfere with what it measures.
why_wrong.B: Participants recalled 40–48% of the idea units a week later, so much of the passage clearly did enter long-term memory; encoding failure would mean the material was never stored.
why_wrong.C: Anterograde amnesia is an inability to form new long-term memories after brain injury; healthy undergraduates forming and retaining memories over a week show normal forgetting, not amnesia.

error_types.A: wrong formula: the measurement cannot interfere with itself
error_types.B: too extreme: partial forgetting mistaken for no storage
error_types.C: out of scope: a clinical condition applied to normal forgetting

items.takeaway: Normal forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows over time (the forgetting curve); good study methods flatten the curve, they do not abolish it.
sources: OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.3 Problems with Memory (2020): Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, storage decay, proactive and retroactive interference, encoding failure, anterograde and retrograde amnesia.
